overview: The Royalty Transparency Act would require federal executive branch employees to publicly report royalties, payments for inventions, that they, their spouses or dependent children receive from inventions the employee developed while working for the government. It would add members of key science and public health advisory panels, such as those that advise on vaccines and biosecurity, to the list of people who must file public financial disclosure reports, along with other public-health advisory committees identified by the Government Accountability Office. Agencies would have to post disclosure reports on their websites, give unredacted copies (except for personal details like addresses and account numbers) to members of Congress on request, and annually publish the names and royalty amounts of employees who file confidential reports. Ethics waivers that let employees work on matters despite a financial conflict would have to be reported to Congress, and conflict-of-interest reviews of federal contractors and grant recipients would have to include royalty payments. As of September 17, 2025, the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee had approved it and it was placed on the Senate calendar.
for: Supporters say the public deserves to know when government scientists and advisers who shape health policy receive money tied to products they helped create, so potential conflicts of interest can be seen and addressed.
against: Critics say publishing the names and royalty income of employees who now file confidentially intrudes on their privacy and could discourage scientists from working for or advising the government.
